title: MirrorFace
summary: MirrorFace, also tracked as Earth Kasha, is an espionage-focused intrusion set whose activity public reporting has linked to Chinese-nexus operations and, in some analyses, to clusters associated with the APT10 ecosystem. Independent vendor reporting has documented sustained targeting of organisations in Japan and in the wider region, including government, research, media and political entities, with campaigns that favour spear phishing, malicious document delivery and abuse of legitimate remote access tools over loud destructive behaviour. Reported tradecraft includes sending email that impersonates a trusted contact or service, using a downloaded document or archive to start a loader, and then deploying backdoors that blend into normal administrator traffic, sometimes through cloud services or web shells on public-facing servers. The group is patient and quiet, so it leaves few obvious symptoms; evidence is found in mail gateway and attachment telemetry, newly created web shells and unusual file writes on internet-facing hosts, authentication logs for remote access tools, and long-lived outbound sessions to infrastructure that does not match the organisation's normal peers.

beginner.definition: MirrorFace is an espionage group, which means it spies instead of asking for money. Security companies also call it Earth Kasha. It sends fake emails and builds fake websites to get onto a computer. Then it stays hidden and reads information for a long time.
beginner.whyItMatters: This kind of attacker wants secrets, not payment. They look at plans, research and private conversations. They often stay for months, so a quick clean up may miss them. If nobody notices, the stolen information can help another country or another company for years. Quiet spying often costs more than a noisy attack.
howItWorks: The group studies a target and writes an email that looks familiar and safe.
The email or a fake website invites the reader to open a file or log in.
Opening it starts a small program that quietly installs a backdoor.
The backdoor calls home through normal services so it looks less strange.
The attackers read mail, documents and plans, and copy what they want.
They keep access ready so they can return even after a clean up.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel night desk. A polite guest in a smart suit asks to leave a parcel for a colleague upstairs. The clerk, wanting to help, carries it to the room. The guest never checks in, but for weeks afterwards someone walks in and out of that floor using the parcel as an excuse. Nobody broke a lock, and everyone remembers the clerk as helpful. MirrorFace enters the same way, with politeness instead of force.
takeaways: Espionage groups want to stay invisible, so absence of alarm is not proof of safety.
Treat unexpected attachments and login pages as suspicious until someone verifies them.
Hunting for long-lived, unusual outbound connections finds quiet intruders better than waiting for alerts.

objectives: Explain what an espionage-motivated intrusion set is and how it differs from a criminal one.
Describe how spear phishing delivers a loader and a backdoor in reported MirrorFace campaigns.
Recognise indicators of a web shell or unusual remote access tool on a public-facing server.
Explain why attribution of this cluster is reported with varying confidence across vendors.
Design detection coverage for long-lived outbound command and control traffic.
Outline an investigation approach for a suspected long-dwell intrusion.
